questions.subtopic: 4D1 Sources of engagement information. An objective about what staff know
questions.question: An engagement at a Chilean mining firm's 60 sites asks whether site staff know how to raise a safety incident under the new policy. Which source BEST serves internal auditor Ignacio?

options.A: A questionnaire asking sampled staff to describe the steps
options.B: The incident log, showing how many reports each site filed
options.C: Site managers' signed checklists confirming staff were briefed
options.D: The approved policy and the training plan that rolled it out

questions.key_concept: Relevance comes from the objective: when the question is what staff know, asking staff to show that knowledge is direct evidence of the condition.
questions.pre_read: What exactly does the objective ask about: what was done, what was planned, or what people know?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.1 makes information relevant when it fits the engagement objective, and its considerations list surveying the people involved. Here the condition is what staff know, so asking sampled staff to describe the steps, and checking each answer against the policy, tests that knowledge directly. Managers' signed checklists, the closest choice, show that briefings were held, not that the people briefed know the route.

wrong_explanations.B: A count of reports filed shows activity, not knowledge. A site with few reports may simply have had few incidents, so the log cannot show what staff know.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the checklists show that briefings happened, as the managers report them. Being briefed is not the same as knowing, and the objective asks about knowledge.
wrong_explanations.D: The policy and training plan describe what should happen. They are the criteria, not evidence of what staff at the 60 sites actually know.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a count of reports shows how often incidents were filed, not whether staff know how, and D, because the policy and plan state the criteria.
Final two: A beats C because the objective is staff knowledge; a questionnaire that asks staff to describe the steps tests it directly, while a checklist records only that a briefing took place.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, let the objective pick the source. When the condition is what people know or believe, asking them is direct evidence, not a weak substitute.

questions.subtopic: 4D2 Judging the quality of evidence. A whole population from an editable file
questions.question: A Kenyan county's procurement head emails internal auditor Wanjiru a spreadsheet of all 4,200 purchase orders, which the head's team maintains; matching every row shows each order approved. Which view is MOST accurate?

options.A: Enough to conclude: every order was tested, not a sample
options.B: Enough to conclude once totals match the team's monthly reports
options.C: Not enough yet: suppliers should confirm each order's delivery
options.D: Not enough yet: the file comes from the team under review

questions.key_concept: A full-population test is only as good as its data: a file kept by the team under review is checked against the source first.
questions.pre_read: Before counting how much was tested, ask who produced the data and whether it could have been changed.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.1 says reliability is strengthened when the internal auditor obtains information directly, or from a system with effective controls, and Standard 4.3 requires critically assessing reliability. A spreadsheet maintained by the team under review is neither, so testing all 4,200 rows adds coverage, not trust. Whole-population testing, the closest choice, is only as good as its data: Wanjiru should take the orders from the purchasing system directly before concluding.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: testing every row removes sampling risk, but not the risk that the rows were altered. Volume never makes up for information that is not yet reliable.
wrong_explanations.B: Both documents come from the same team, so agreement between them is not independent corroboration. A file and reports from one source can match and both be wrong.
wrong_explanations.C: Delivery confirmations bear on whether goods arrived, not on whether orders were approved. They come from an outside party, but they do not fit this objective.

tips: Eliminate: B, because two records from the same team do not corroborate each other independently, and C, because delivery evidence does not answer whether orders were approved.
Final two: D beats A because Standard 14.1 ties reliability to who obtained the data and the system behind it; testing every row of the team's own spreadsheet tests the file, not the orders.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, a full-population test inherits the quality of its data. Ask who produced the file and whether it could be changed before trusting the count.

questions.subtopic: 4D2 Judging the quality of evidence. A first-hand extract from a weakly controlled system
questions.question: Internal auditor Rangi queried a New Zealand hospital's pharmacy stock system directly; a review last month found staff can overwrite quantities with no log or review. Which view of the results is MOST accurate?

options.A: Strong: Rangi obtained the quantities first-hand from the system
options.B: Weakened: the system behind them lacks effective controls
options.C: Weakened: the data came from the activity's own system
options.D: Strong: the figures are current and come from the official record

questions.key_concept: Reliability has three separate factors; getting data first-hand does not repair figures held in a system whose controls over changes are missing.
questions.pre_read: Check each reliability factor on its own: who obtained the data, what corroborates it, and how well controlled its source system is.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.1 names three things that strengthen reliability: the internal auditor obtaining information directly or from an independent source, corroboration, and a system with effective governance, risk management and control processes. Rangi's first-hand query meets the first, but quantities anyone can overwrite unseen fail the third, so the figures need corroboration, such as a count, before use. First-hand retrieval, the closest choice, cannot repair weak data at its source.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: obtaining data directly does strengthen reliability, but only for how it was retrieved. Quantities that staff can change unseen may be wrong before Rangi's query runs.
wrong_explanations.C: Querying the activity's own system is normal. Rangi obtained the data directly, which meets the first factor; the weakness is the missing control over changes.
wrong_explanations.D: Current, official figures are reliable only when the system that holds them is well controlled. Here last month's review found the controls over changes missing.

tips: Eliminate: C, because a direct query of the activity's own system meets the first reliability factor, and D, because official figures are only as good as the controls over them.
Final two: B beats A because Standard 14.1 counts the system behind the data as its own reliability factor; retrieving it first-hand does not fix figures anyone can overwrite.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, test all three reliability factors separately: who obtained it, what corroborates it, and how well controlled its source system is.

questions.subtopic: 4D2 Judging the quality of evidence. A sample the activity selected
questions.question: Internal auditor Kasia tested 25 of a Polish retailer's 610 vendor master changes, the size the methodology sets; the vendor team lead selected them, and all were authorized. Which view is MOST accurate?

options.A: Too weak for the 610: the audited unit, not Kasia, chose them
options.B: Too weak for the 610: 25 items cannot represent so many changes
options.C: Enough for the 610: each tested change carried the required approval
options.D: Enough for the 610: another auditor could repeat Kasia's 25 tests

questions.key_concept: Sufficient means a competent reviewer would reach the same conclusion about the whole population, which a sample the audited team chose may not represent.
questions.pre_read: Ask what population the conclusion covers, and whether the items tested were chosen so that they stand for it.
questions.correct_explanation: Under Standard 14.1, evidence is sufficient when someone careful, informed and capable could redo the work program and arrive at the same conclusions, and its considerations say a sample should be as representative of the population as possible. Items the audited team picked may leave out the changes that matter. Repeating the 25 tests, the closest choice, would only confirm those 25; it says nothing yet about the other 585.

wrong_explanations.B: The methodology sets 25 for this population, so size is not the gap. A sample of that size can support a conclusion when it is chosen to represent all changes.
wrong_explanations.C: The tests show those 25 were authorized. A clean result speaks for all 610 only if the sample represents them.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: repeatability is part of the test, but the reviewer must also reach the same conclusion about all 610. Redoing a hand-picked sample does not get there.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the methodology already sets 25 for this population, and C, because a clean result on 25 items speaks for all 610 only if they represent the rest.
Final two: A beats D because Standard 14.1's reviewer must reach the same conclusion, not just the same 25 results; a sample the audited team chose may not represent the year.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about sufficiency, ask who chose the items and what population they stand for. A sample supports only what it represents.

questions.subtopic: 4D4 Analytics and process mapping. A walk-through that contradicts the approved map
questions.question: At a Turkish retailer, management's approved map shows a supervisor approving every credit note; internal auditor Elif's walk-through of three notes found none approved. What is the BEST basis for the condition?

options.A: The approved map, treating the three credit notes as exceptions
options.B: How the three credit notes were handled when followed through
options.C: The process the billing clerks describe when interviewed
options.D: The billing policy on which credit notes need approval

questions.key_concept: The condition is what evidence shows the process does; a map, however approved, shows the design management intends.
questions.pre_read: Which of these shows how the process is meant to run, and which shows how it actually runs?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.2 requires the condition to be determined from information and evidence gathered during the engagement. Following real credit notes through the process is first-hand evidence of how it runs, so the observed practice is the condition. The approved map, the closest choice, shows how management says the process should run; calling three unapproved notes exceptions assumes a result the testing has not shown.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: an approved map shows the intended design, which can inform the criteria. Three walk-throughs that all contradict it are evidence about the condition, not exceptions to set aside.
wrong_explanations.C: What clerks describe is a statement that needs corroboration. The walk-through has already shown the real practice, so the clerks' account cannot override it.
wrong_explanations.D: The policy says which notes need approval, which makes it criteria. The condition is what actually happens, and that comes from evidence.

tips: Eliminate: C, because interview statements need corroboration and cannot outweigh what was observed, and D, because a policy sets the criteria, not the condition.
Final two: B beats A because Standard 14.2 sets the condition from evidence gathered; an approved map is management's design, and three contrary walk-throughs are evidence, not exceptions.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, a process map is a claim about design until real items are walked through it. Condition comes from evidence; criteria from what should be.

questions.subtopic: 4D4 Analytics and process mapping. Entries flagged by anomaly detection
questions.question: Anomaly detection on a Vietnamese manufacturer's 90,000 journal entries flags 160 as out of pattern, such as weekend postings. Which next step is BEST for internal auditor Linh?

options.A: Log the 160 as potential findings, then ask staff to explain each
options.B: Ask the controller to reverse the 160 entries before closing
options.C: Run the same detection on last year's entries for comparison
options.D: Check each of the 160 against the posting policy and its support

questions.key_concept: An analytics flag shows an entry is unusual; it becomes a potential finding only when evidence shows it differs from the criteria.
questions.pre_read: Is an unusual entry the same thing as an entry that breaks a rule?
questions.correct_explanation: Under Standard 14.2, a potential finding is a gap between what the criteria require and the condition the evidence shows. An entry flagged as unusual has broken a pattern, not yet a rule: a weekend posting may be allowed. Checking each against the posting policy and its support shows which ones differ from the criteria. Logging all 160 as potential findings first, the closest choice, treats the tool's pattern as the criteria.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: following up is right, but labeling all 160 as potential findings first treats unusual as wrong. Only a difference from the criteria makes a potential finding.
wrong_explanations.B: Correcting entries is management's decision, and only once an entry is shown to be wrong. Reversing entries no one has examined could undo valid postings.
wrong_explanations.C: A second year's flags would show whether the pattern is new, which can help later. It cannot show whether any of these 160 entries breaks the posting policy.

tips: Eliminate: B, because correcting entries is management's call once an error is shown, and C, because another year's flags say nothing about whether these 160 break the policy.
Final two: D beats A because Standard 14.2 makes a potential finding a difference from the criteria; a flag only shows an entry is unusual until it is checked against the rule.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, an analytics flag is a lead. It becomes a potential finding only when evidence shows the condition differs from the criteria.

questions.subtopic: 4D4 Analytics and process mapping. An answer held in unstructured contract text
questions.question: Internal auditor Thandi must learn whether a South African miner's supplier contracts hold an anti-bribery clause; each contract is stored as a text file, with fields for dates, values and parties. Which analysis BEST fits?

options.A: Query the system's structured fields, which cover every contract
options.B: Read 30 contract files from the largest unit, clause by clause
options.C: Search every contract file for the clause's key wording
options.D: Ask each contract owner to confirm the clause is included

questions.key_concept: Find where the answer is recorded before choosing the method: when it sits in free text, text analysis of the unstructured data fits.
questions.pre_read: Which data source could actually show whether a contract contains the clause?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.1 requires information consistent with the engagement objective. The question is what each contract says, and the fields hold only dates, values and parties, so the answer sits in the contract files: unstructured data that text analysis can search for the clause's wording across every contract. Querying the structured fields, the closest choice, uses complete, tidy data that cannot show whether the clause is there.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the structured fields cover every contract, but none records the clause. Complete data that does not hold the answer is not relevant to this objective.
wrong_explanations.B: Reading contracts is the right source, but 30 from one unit cannot speak for every contract. A search of every file covers the whole population at little cost.
wrong_explanations.D: Owners' confirmations are statements from the people responsible for the contracts. The contracts themselves are on file, so Thandi can examine them first-hand.

tips: Eliminate: B, because 30 contracts from one unit do not represent all contracts, and D, because owners' confirmations are statements when the contracts can be examined first-hand.
Final two: C beats A because Standard 14.1 asks for information that fits the objective; the fields cover every contract but hold nothing about the clause, which sits in the contract files.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, find where the answer is recorded before picking the method. Free text is unstructured data, and text analysis is how to read it at scale.

questions.subtopic: 4D5 Analytical review techniques. An independent headcount for the expectation
questions.question: Internal auditor Paola builds an expectation for a Mexican retailer's 12% payroll cost rise from the pay award and average headcount; HR keeps staff records apart from payroll. Which headcount source BEST serves the test?

options.A: The payroll system's count, as it covers the people being paid
options.B: Last year's count plus planned hires, as the budget used them
options.C: The payroll manager's estimate, as the manager knows the staff
options.D: The HR records' count, as HR records each hire and leaver

questions.key_concept: An analytical expectation needs drivers from a source independent of the figure tested; a payroll headcount rises with any false employees.
questions.pre_read: If someone added false employees to payroll, which headcount would rise with the cost, and which would not?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.2's considerations include relating payroll expense to the average number of employees, and Standard 14.1 says information is more reliable when it comes from an independent source or is corroborated. HR records kept apart from payroll can expose a cost rise that headcount does not explain. The payroll system's own count, the closest choice, would rise with any false employees added to payroll, so the expectation would hide the gap it should reveal.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the payroll count does cover the people paid, which is the problem: any false employee added to payroll raises cost and count together, so the gap disappears.
wrong_explanations.B: Planned hires show what the budget expected, not who was actually employed. An expectation built on them tests payroll against the plan, not against reality.
wrong_explanations.C: An estimate from the manager responsible for payroll is a statement from the activity under review. It is neither independent nor a record of who was employed.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the payroll manager's estimate is a statement from the activity under review, and B, because planned hires show the budget, not who was actually employed.
Final two: D beats A because Standard 14.1 favors information from an independent source; a headcount drawn from payroll itself moves with the cost it is meant to test.
Exam cue: on CIA analytical review questions, take the drivers of an expectation from a source independent of the figure being tested, or the comparison can hide the problem.

questions.subtopic: 4D6 Findings and their significance. Stating the effect when no loss has occurred
questions.question: At a Philippine lender, internal auditor Marisol finds 14 loan officers can change borrowers' bank details without review; tests found no misuse this year. Which BEST states the finding's effect?

options.A: Payouts could be redirected to accounts that no one has checked
options.B: None so far, since tests found no misuse during the year
options.C: The breach of the policy requiring review of detail changes
options.D: The cost management could incur to add a review step

questions.key_concept: A finding's effect is the potential exposure the gap creates; it exists while the gap is open, whether or not a loss has happened.
questions.pre_read: Keep the parts of a finding apart: criteria, condition, root cause and effect. Which one is each option describing?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.3 requires internal auditors to determine the potential effects of each potential finding, and its considerations describe the effect as the risk or potential exposure, often estimated with input from management. Payouts that could go to accounts no one checks are that exposure, whether or not misuse has happened yet. No effect, the closest choice, confuses what has happened with what could happen.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: no misuse found is good news, but the effect is the potential exposure. A gap that could let payouts be redirected matters before any loss occurs.
wrong_explanations.C: Unreviewed changes measured against the policy are the condition and the criteria of the finding. The effect is what that gap could cause.
wrong_explanations.D: The cost of a fix matters when weighing recommendations or action plans. It is not the effect of the gap.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the gap between policy and practice is the condition against the criteria, and D, because the cost of a fix belongs to weighing the action, not the effect.
Final two: A beats B because Standard 14.3 asks for potential effects; an exposure exists while the gap is open, whether or not a loss has occurred yet.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, keep the parts of a finding apart: criteria (what should be), condition (what is), root cause (why) and effect (what could result).

questions.subtopic: 4D6 Findings and their significance. Ranking findings with the function's methodology
questions.question: Internal auditor Javier finds the function's rating scale too coarse for a Spanish port's engagement, and the port's manager asks that findings be ranked by cost to fix. How should Javier BEST rank them?

options.A: By the cost to fix, as the port's manager requests
options.B: By the money at stake, the measure the board reads most easily
options.C: On a finer scale fitted to this engagement, explained in the report
options.D: On the existing scale, with the concern raised separately

questions.key_concept: Findings are ranked with the chief audit executive's methodology so ratings stay consistent across engagements; a better method is proposed, not used alone.
questions.pre_read: Who sets the method for rating findings, and what would a different scale do to comparisons with other engagements?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.3 requires each finding to be ranked by significance with the chief audit executive's methodology, and its considerations say this keeps ratings consistent across engagements. Javier rates on the function's scale and takes the view that it is too coarse to the chief audit executive, who owns the method. A scale fitted to this engagement, the closest choice, sounds careful but makes these ratings mean something different from every other engagement's.

wrong_explanations.A: Cost to fix can help management order its action plans. Significance rests on likelihood and impact, so the manager's preference does not set the ranking.
wrong_explanations.B: Money is one part of impact. Significance also weighs likelihood and other factors, so ranking by money alone can misrank a small but serious gap.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: a finer scale may describe this engagement better, but Standard 14.3 requires the chief audit executive's methodology. A private scale breaks consistency across engagements.

tips: Eliminate: A, because significance rests on likelihood and impact rather than the cost of a fix, and B, because money alone leaves out likelihood and the nature of the risk.
Final two: D beats C because Standard 14.3 requires prioritizing with the chief audit executive's methodology; a better scale is proposed to the chief audit executive, not used alone.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, the internal auditor applies the function's methodology and proposes changes to it; changing it alone for one engagement is the trap.

questions.subtopic: 4D7 Workpapers that support the results. A workpaper with no population or selection
questions.question: Internal auditor Tomas's workpaper on an Israeli insurer's claim payments lists the 60 claims tested, what was checked on each, the 4 exceptions and Tomas's initials. What does it MOST need before review?

options.A: The claims manager's sign-off on the 4 exceptions
options.B: The population and the method used to pick the sample
options.C: The engagement risk assessment behind this test
options.D: A cross-reference to the work program step this test completes

questions.key_concept: A complete workpaper lets another competent auditor repeat the test, which needs the population and how items were selected, not only the results.
questions.pre_read: Could another auditor redo this test from the file alone, and if not, what is missing?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.6 requires work to be documented well enough that another informed, careful internal auditor could redo it and get the same results, and its considerations list the population, sample size and selection method in a workpaper's basic format. Without them, no one could repeat the selection. A cross-reference to the work program, the closest choice, points to the planned approach, not the population actually tested or how the sample was drawn.

wrong_explanations.A: Discussing exceptions with management is part of the work, but the manager's agreement does not show where the 60 came from or let anyone repeat the test.
wrong_explanations.C: The risk assessment belongs in the engagement file and explains why the test exists. It does not record how the 60 claims were chosen.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a cross-reference is useful, and the work program states the planned sampling, but only the workpaper shows the population actually tested and how these 60 were drawn.

tips: Eliminate: A, because management's agreement on exceptions does not show how the claims were chosen, and C, because the risk assessment explains why the test exists, not how it was done.
Final two: B beats D because Standard 14.6 requires enough to repeat the work; the work program shows the plan, while the workpaper's population and selection let someone redo this test.
Exam cue: on CIA workpaper questions, apply the stranger test: could another competent auditor redo the work from the file alone and get the same result?

questions.subtopic: 4D8 Reaching engagement conclusions. Minor gaps that together weaken one control aim
questions.question: In an engagement on a Jordanian airport's three fuel-loss controls, internal auditor Bilal found a low-rated gap in each: late counts, unreconciled meter readings, unreviewed loss reports. On a two-level scale, which conclusion is BEST?

options.A: Satisfactory, since each finding on its own is rated low
options.B: Unsatisfactory, as together the gaps weaken each loss check
options.C: Satisfactory, with the gaps reported as one finding on losses
options.D: Unsatisfactory, since three findings are too many to overlook

questions.key_concept: The conclusion weighs findings together: minor gaps that weaken every control over one aim can add up to an unsatisfactory conclusion.
questions.pre_read: Look past each finding's own rating: what do the three gaps have in common, and what does that mean taken together?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.5 requires the conclusion to state the internal auditors' judgment of how significant the findings are taken together. Each gap looks minor alone, but all three loss controls are weakened at once, so none can make up for another, and on a two-level scale the processes cannot be called effective. Reporting one combined finding while concluding satisfactory, the closest choice, weighs the gaps in a finding but not in the conclusion.

wrong_explanations.A: Rating each finding alone is the first step, not the conclusion. Standard 14.5 asks for the overall significance of the findings taken together.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: combining the gaps shows the right instinct, but a satisfactory verdict says the processes work while every loss check is weakened. The conclusion must carry the aggregate judgment.
wrong_explanations.D: The verdict follows the findings' combined significance, not their number. Three low findings on unrelated matters could still fit a satisfactory conclusion.

tips: Eliminate: A, because rating findings one by one is not weighing them together, and D, because the verdict follows combined significance, not the number of findings.
Final two: B beats C because Standard 14.5 puts the aggregate judgment in the conclusion itself; a combined finding beside a satisfactory verdict leaves the conclusion unweighed.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, weigh findings, do not count them: minor gaps that hit the same objective can add up to an unsatisfactory conclusion, and many unrelated ones need not.

questions.subtopic: 4D8 Reaching engagement conclusions. A conclusion that only lists findings
questions.question: Internal auditor Mei's draft conclusion for an assurance engagement on a Taiwanese chipmaker's payroll lists three rated findings with their root causes, and stops there. What does it MOST lack?

options.A: Management's action plans, with owners and due dates
options.B: A statement that the work conformed with the Standards
options.C: A judgment on how well the controls work, taken as a whole
options.D: An overall rating equal to its highest-rated finding

questions.key_concept: An assurance conclusion is the auditor's overall judgment on how effective governance, risk management and controls are; a list of findings is not a conclusion.
questions.pre_read: Which of these belongs in the conclusion itself, and which belongs elsewhere in the final communication?
questions.correct_explanation: Under Standard 14.5, an assurance conclusion sums up the results against the engagement's objectives and management's, and says how effective the activity's governance, risk management and control processes are. A list of rated findings leaves that judgment unstated. Action plans with owners and dates, the closest choice, are required in the final communication under Standard 15.1, but they are not part of the conclusion.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: Standard 15.1 requires owners and dates in the final communication, but they record management's response. The conclusion is the internal auditor's own overall judgment.
wrong_explanations.B: The final communication should carry a conformance statement when supervision and the quality program support it. It is not part of the conclusion, the auditor's overall judgment.
wrong_explanations.D: A methodology may give the conclusion a rating, but Standard 14.5 asks for judgment on the findings together and on the controls' effectiveness, not a copy of the worst rating.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a conformance statement belongs to the final communication, not the conclusion, and D, because copying the worst rating replaces the judgment the conclusion must state.
Final two: C beats A because Standard 14.5 makes the effectiveness judgment part of an assurance conclusion; owners and dates are final communication content under Standard 15.1.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, a list of findings is not a conclusion. An assurance conclusion says how well the processes work, including when they work.

questions.subtopic: 4D9 Supervising the engagement. Closer review for an expert in a new, complex area
questions.question: Supervisor Farah plans light review for senior auditor Joaquín, who has 12 years of payroll audits and recent derivatives training, on a Peruvian bank's complex derivative-valuation engagement. What is Farah's BEST course?

options.A: Keep the light review, since Joaquín's experience sets how close it is
options.B: Bring in a valuation specialist to redo Joaquín's tests
options.C: Review Joaquín's valuation work closely from planning to sign-off
options.D: Keep the light review, adding a checklist sign-off on each workpaper

questions.key_concept: Supervision depth follows the function's maturity, the auditor's experience and the work's complexity together; years in another area do not cover a new, complex one.
questions.pre_read: Supervision depth turns on more than one factor. Which of them does this stem change, and which does it leave alone?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 12.3 Oversee and Improve Engagement Performance ties the extent of supervision to the function's maturity, the auditor's proficiency and experience, and the engagement's complexity. Joaquín's experience is in payroll, with only training in valuations, and the engagement is complex, so closer review fits. Keeping light review, the runner-up, counts years in another area as experience in this one and passes over complexity.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: experience is one factor in the extent of supervision, but Joaquín's is in payroll, and Standard 12.3 also weighs the engagement's complexity, which is high here.
wrong_explanations.B: A specialist fills a competency the team lacks. Joaquín has the training, so the need is closer supervision of the work, not a second party redoing it.
wrong_explanations.D: Standard 12.3's considerations offer checklists where no supervisor is available. Here a supervisor is, and complexity calls for closer review; a checklist on light review does not supply it.

tips: Eliminate: B, because Joaquín has the training, so redoing the tests answers a competency gap that is not there, and D, because a checklist supports oversight; it does not deepen light review.
Final two: C beats A because experience counts in the area being audited, and complexity also sets the extent of supervision; here both point to closer review.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about how closely to supervise, check all three factors: the function's maturity, the auditor's experience in this area, and the engagement's complexity.

questions.subtopic: 4D9 Supervising the engagement. A conclusion wider than the tests behind it
questions.question: Checking workpapers on a Tunisian retailer's stock engagement, supervisor Karim reads auditor Salma's conclusion that all six warehouses reconcile stock monthly; Salma tested the two nearest. What is Karim's BEST response?

options.A: Sign off, since both tested warehouses reconcile monthly
options.B: Narrow the draft report's conclusion to the two warehouses tested
options.C: Have Salma get written confirmations from the other four managers
options.D: Raise a review note questioning the conclusion's reach past the tests

questions.key_concept: A conclusion wider than its evidence goes back through a review note: the auditor widens the tests or narrows the conclusion in the workpapers.
questions.pre_read: What do two warehouses' tests support, and where does a supervisor's doubt get resolved: in the workpapers or in the draft?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 12.3 Oversee and Improve Engagement Performance has the supervisor confirm that workpapers support the conclusions, and its considerations let the supervisor ask for more evidence or clarification. Two warehouses picked for nearness do not support a claim about six, so a review note sends it back: Salma widens the tests or narrows the conclusion, and the workpapers change. Narrowing the draft, the runner-up, leaves the unsupported workpaper behind.

wrong_explanations.A: Passing tests at two warehouses support a conclusion about those two. The supervisor confirms the workpapers support the conclusion as written, and these do not support all six.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the claim must narrow or the evidence widen, but workpapers are the primary support for communications; the review note gets them amended before any draft changes.
wrong_explanations.C: Confirmations from the managers responsible for the warehouses are weaker evidence than tests (Standard 14.1), and they would not show four warehouses' reconciliations work.

tips: Eliminate: A, because two warehouses' results cannot support a conclusion about six, and C, because statements from the managers responsible are weaker evidence than the auditor's own tests.
Final two: D beats B because workpapers are the primary support for any communication; a review note gets them amended, by more tests or a narrower conclusion, before the draft changes.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about a supervisor's review, doubts go back to the auditor through review notes for evidence or clarification; the supervisor does not edit the result alone.

questions.subtopic: 4D9 Supervising the engagement. Supervising a cosourced firm's tests
questions.question: Internal audit at a Thai airline cosources an engagement's IT tests to a certified firm under the approved program; the firm offers its own quality review instead of supervision. What is supervisor Niran's BEST response?

options.A: Review the firm's workpapers for support, as for staff work
options.B: Accept the firm's quality review, as the firm is certified
options.C: Have the firm adopt the function's methodology for its IT tests
options.D: Repeat the firm's IT tests with staff before using the results

questions.key_concept: Engagement work done by an outside service provider is supervised like staff work; the chief audit executive stays responsible, whoever performs it.
questions.pre_read: Are these tests part of internal audit's own engagement, or another provider's separate work? The answer sets the duty.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 12.3 Oversee and Improve Engagement Performance makes the chief audit executive responsible for supervising engagements whether staff or other service providers do the work; supervision may be delegated, but responsibility stays. So Niran reviews the firm's workpapers as for staff. Accepting the firm's own review, the runner-up, fits relying on another assurance provider's separate work under Standard 9.5, not tests done inside this engagement.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: Standard 9.5 lets the chief audit executive rely, on a documented basis, on other providers' separate work. These tests sit inside the engagement, so they are supervised.
wrong_explanations.C: Working to the function's methodology helps, but it does not replace supervision: the chief audit executive stays responsible for supervising work that service providers do (Standard 12.3).
wrong_explanations.D: Reperforming suits work whose competence or care is in doubt. Supervision means reviewing the workpapers for support; nothing here suggests the firm's tests need redoing.

tips: Eliminate: C, because working to the function's methodology does not replace supervision of the work, and D, because nothing suggests the tests need redoing; reviewing them is the duty.
Final two: A beats B because work a service provider does inside the engagement is supervised like staff work; relying on another provider's own separate work is a different case.
Exam cue: on CIA questions with outside help, ask whether the work sits inside the engagement (supervise it) or is another provider's separate work (evaluate it and document the reliance).

questions.subtopic: 4D10 Communicating during the engagement. A timing change with the scope unchanged
questions.question: A system freeze pushes auditor Wanjiru's fieldwork in a Kenyan water utility's billing unit two weeks later; objectives, scope, work program and budgeted hours stay unchanged. Which step is Wanjiru MOST clearly required to take?

options.A: Get the chief audit executive's approval before changing the dates
options.B: Ask billing management to agree to the new dates first
options.C: Tell billing management about the new dates promptly
options.D: Note the new dates, and tell management at the closing meeting

questions.key_concept: Every change to an engagement's timing is communicated with management timely; approval is needed for changes to the objectives, scope or work program.
questions.pre_read: List what changed and what stayed the same. Which changes need approval, and which need only to be communicated?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.1 Engagement Communication requires internal auditors to communicate the objectives, scope and timing with management, and to communicate later changes timely. Telling billing management promptly meets it. Approval by the chief audit executive, the runner-up, is required for changes to the objectives and scope (Standard 13.3) and to the work program (Standard 13.6); here only the dates move.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the chief audit executive approves changes to objectives, scope and the work program, but none of those changes here. A timing change must be communicated with management timely.
wrong_explanations.B: Standard 13.1 requires the new dates to be communicated with management, not agreed by it. Seeking management's support is sound, but its agreement is not a precondition in assurance work.
wrong_explanations.D: Recording the change is sound, but Standard 13.1 requires changes to be communicated timely; the closing meeting comes too late for a schedule management must plan around.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the new dates must be communicated with management, not first agreed by it, and D, because a change held for the closing meeting is not communicated timely.
Final two: C beats A because approval covers changes to objectives, scope and the work program; a change in timing alone must be communicated with management timely.

Exam cue: on CIA questions about a change mid-engagement, ask what changed: objectives, scope or work program need approval; a change to objectives, scope or timing is communicated with management timely.

questions.subtopic: 4D10 Communicating during the engagement. An opening meeting declined, email instead
questions.question: Auditor Ignacio has finished the risk assessment for a Chilean winery's export-rebate assurance engagement, but the export manager, traveling for a month, declines any meeting and asks for email instead. What is Ignacio's BEST response?

options.A: Delay fieldwork until the export manager can attend a meeting
options.B: Email the risk results, objectives, scope and timing, and file it
options.C: Email the objectives, scope and timing; save risk results for the closing
options.D: Have the chief audit executive treat the refusal as a scope limitation

questions.key_concept: Objectives, scope and timing must reach management; a meeting is the preferred way to share them with the risk results, not a requirement.
questions.pre_read: Separate what must reach the manager from the way it is preferably delivered. Which of the two does the refusal affect?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.1 Engagement Communication requires the objectives, scope and timing to be communicated with management; its considerations add the risk assessment results, preferably in a meeting, and a record in the workpapers. A meeting is preferred, not required, so a filed email carries what the manager must hear. Delaying fieldwork, the runner-up, treats the preference as a condition and loses a month.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a meeting is the preferred way to share risk results, objectives and scope, but it is not required; an email carries the same content without a month's delay.
wrong_explanations.C: Risk assessment results should be shared once the assessment is done, with the objectives and scope (Standard 13.1); the closing communication is for finalizing engagement results.
wrong_explanations.D: A scope limitation is a condition that stops the planned work, such as refused access. Declining a meeting while answering by email blocks no planned test.

tips: Eliminate: C, because risk results should be shared once the assessment is done, not held for the closing, and D, because declining a meeting blocks no planned work, so it is no scope limitation.
Final two: B beats A because the content must reach management and a meeting is only the preferred way; email meets the requirement where a meeting cannot happen.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, separate what must be communicated from the preferred way to do it: when the preferred form fails, deliver the required content another way and keep a record.

questions.subtopic: 4D10 Communicating during the engagement. Who decides that a matter reaches the board
questions.question: Mid-fieldwork, auditor Aiman finds a Malaysian refinery safety risk that may exceed the board's risk tolerance, and alerts plant management at once. Who is MOST appropriately placed to decide whether the board hears of it?

options.A: Aiman, who judges the finding's significance
options.B: Senior management, which works with the board on escalation
options.C: The plant manager, who owns the risk and its response
options.D: The chief audit executive, applying criteria set with the board

questions.key_concept: The auditor judges significance and raises the facts; the chief audit executive decides what reaches the board, under escalation criteria agreed with the board.
questions.pre_read: Separate two judgments: how significant the finding is, and whether the board hears of it. Who holds each one?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 8.1 Board Interaction makes the chief audit executive responsible for giving the board what it needs, and its essential conditions have the board set expectations with the chief audit executive for which issues are escalated, such as significant risks beyond its tolerance. So the chief audit executive decides, applying those criteria. Aiman, the runner-up, judges significance under Standard 14.3, then brings the facts up the line.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: Aiman judges the finding's significance (Standard 14.3), but escalation to the board runs through the chief audit executive, who applies the criteria agreed with the board.
wrong_explanations.B: Senior management helps the board and the chief audit executive shape how matters are escalated, but it does not decide what internal audit takes to the board.
wrong_explanations.C: The plant manager owns the risk and chooses the response. Owning a risk does not include deciding whether internal audit's concerns about it reach the board.

tips: Eliminate: B, because senior management helps shape the escalation process but does not filter internal audit's reports, and C, because owning the risk means choosing the response, not deciding what the board hears.
Final two: D beats A because the auditor judges significance and raises it, but the chief audit executive takes matters to the board under the criteria agreed with it.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about reaching the board, the internal auditor raises the facts; the chief audit executive applies the board's escalation criteria and goes to the board.

questions.subtopic: 4D10 Communicating during the engagement. Who hears a finding during fieldwork
questions.question: Auditing a Uruguayan hotel chain's rate controls, auditor Lucía finds front-desk staff making unapproved overrides of rules the revenue director owns; their supervisor offers to agree a fix. What is Lucía's BEST course?

options.A: Discuss the finding and possible fixes with the revenue director
options.B: Agree a fix with the front-desk supervisor, then copy the director
options.C: Raise the finding with the director at the closing meeting
options.D: Discuss the finding first with the chain's general manager

questions.key_concept: Findings and possible actions are discussed promptly with the management authorized to change the activity; supervisors below it can confirm facts, not settle the fix.
questions.pre_read: Who owns the rules being broken? Then ask whether the offer, the timing or the rank of the listener changes that.
questions.correct_explanation: The considerations to Standard 14.4 Recommendations and Action Plans say findings and possible recommendations should be discussed promptly with the managers who have authority to change and oversee the activity. The override rules are the revenue director's, so Lucía discusses them there, though the supervisor offers to settle it. Agreeing a fix with the supervisor, the runner-up, settles actions with someone who can confirm facts but does not own the rules.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the supervisor can confirm facts and help find causes, and a copy informs the director, but actions are discussed with the management that owns the rules.
wrong_explanations.C: The closing communication finalizes results; findings should be discussed promptly so management can act, and nothing here justifies waiting until the end.
wrong_explanations.D: The general manager oversees the whole chain, but the director owns the override rules. Findings go first to the management directly authorized to change the activity.

tips: Eliminate: C, because findings are discussed promptly, not held for the closing communication, and D, because the most senior manager is not the one who owns these rules.
Final two: A beats B because findings and actions are discussed with the management that owns the rules; the supervisor can confirm facts, and a copy does not make the director a party.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about who hears a finding, pick the manager with authority over the activity: not the staff who did the work, and not simply the most senior person.

questions.subtopic: 4D3 Technology tools for audit work. A checked model that flags nothing
questions.question: Internal auditor Ana's model, validated on known duplicate claims, checked all 52,000 of a Brazilian insurer's claims for the year in scope, reconciled to the ledger, and flagged none. What is Ana's BEST next step?

options.A: Conclude that the model's run found no duplicate payment
options.B: Hand-test a random sample of claims to confirm the result
options.C: Run the model on last year's claims too, before concluding
options.D: Have the claims team run the model monthly as its own check

questions.key_concept: Once a tool's logic is validated and its data reconciled, its full-population result is sufficient; rechecking a subset adds cost for little benefit.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the tool's result still lacks: were its logic and its data both checked? If so, what would more testing add?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.1 strengthens reliability when data is corroborated, and the ledger reconciliation did that; testing the model on known duplicates showed its logic works. Its run over the whole year lets another competent auditor repeat the work and reach the same result. Standard 4.2 weighs cost against benefit, so a hand sample, the closest choice, adds cost for little benefit, and Standard 14.2 then calls for assurance in the conclusion.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a hand sample helps when a tool's logic or data is untested. Both were checked here, so a sample adds cost for little benefit (Standard 4.2).
wrong_explanations.C: The objective covers the year in scope. Last year's claims fall outside it, so running them adds work no objective asks for and delays the conclusion.
wrong_explanations.D: Handing management a monitoring routine is a possible later recommendation, not the step that completes this test. With a clean, reliable result, the next step is the conclusion (Standard 14.2).

tips: Eliminate: C, because last year's claims sit outside the year in scope, and D, because a monitoring routine for management is a later recommendation, not the step that completes this test.
Final two: A beats B because the model's logic and data were both checked; under Standard 4.2, a hand sample of the same records costs more than the little it adds.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, check a tool's logic and data before relying on it; once both pass, its full-population result can carry the conclusion without a manual backup.

questions.subtopic: 4D6 Findings and their significance. Two exceptions in a sample of fifteen
questions.question: Internal auditor Rosa's approved program tests 15 of a Peruvian university's grant payments over $20,000 for a second approver's sign-off; 2 of the 15 lack it. What is Rosa's BEST next step?

options.A: Report the two as a finding, rated on the function's scale
options.B: Test 45 more payments now, under the approved program as it stands
options.C: Note the two as a potential finding, then start the next test
options.D: Evaluate the two for cause, effect and any need for more tests

questions.key_concept: A difference from criteria is a potential finding to evaluate; more testing follows only if due care calls for it, through an approved program change.
questions.pre_read: Two items differ from the criteria. Before reporting or testing more, what do the Standards ask the auditor to do with a difference?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.2 requires a difference between criteria and condition to be noted as a potential finding and then evaluated, and Standard 14.3 makes that evaluation the cause, effect and significance. Due care also decides whether the evidence needs more tests, which would go into an approved program change. Recording the two and moving on, the closest choice, notes the difference but leaves the evaluation undone.

wrong_explanations.A: Reporting comes after evaluation: Standard 14.3 asks for cause, effect and significance first, and two of fifteen payments do not yet show how far the gap reaches.
wrong_explanations.B: Under Standard 14.2, added testing needs an adjusted work program approved by the chief audit executive or a delegate; testing now under the unchanged program skips that step.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: Standard 14.2 requires the difference to be noted and then evaluated, including whether this test needs more evidence. Moving on leaves cause, effect and that decision unsettled.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a potential finding is evaluated for cause, effect and significance before it is reported, and B, because added testing needs an adjusted, approved work program.
Final two: D beats C because Standard 14.2 requires a difference to be noted and then evaluated; recording it and moving on stops at the first step.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, a difference from criteria is noted, then evaluated; whether to test more is a due-care decision, and any added testing changes the program.

questions.subtopic: 4D7 Workpapers that support the results. A cause that rests on the manager's account
questions.question: Tracing a draft finding on a Ugandan coffee depot's stock losses to the workpapers, internal auditor Mukasa checks the basis of each part. Which part MOST needs more support before review?

options.A: The rating, set on the function's scale, which the depot manager disputes
options.B: The shortfall, from an independent stocktaker's count Mukasa arranged
options.C: The cause, a scanner fault since March, as the manager described it
options.D: The loss, an estimate Mukasa made with the depot's accountant

questions.key_concept: Identifying a root cause with management does not make management's account evidence: the cause in a finding needs corroborating support in the workpapers.
questions.pre_read: For each part of the finding, ask where its support came from and whether another auditor could verify it from the file.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.6 requires the evidence behind engagement results to be documented, and Standard 4.3 calls for more evidence on statements that may be incomplete or false. A manager blaming losses on equipment is such a statement: working out root causes with management, as Standard 14.3 asks, does not make the manager's account the evidence. A disputed rating, the closest choice, rests on the function's scale; disagreement alone is not missing support.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a dispute calls for discussion, not more evidence by itself. Standard 13.1 does not oblige a change without a valid reason, and the rating follows the function's scale.
wrong_explanations.B: A count by an independent stocktaker Mukasa arranged is information from an independent source, which Standard 14.1 says strengthens reliability, so the shortfall rests on solid support.
wrong_explanations.D: An estimated loss is normal: Standard 14.3 notes that exposure is often an estimate the auditor makes with input from the activity's management.

tips: Eliminate: B, because an independent stocktaker's count is a source Standard 14.1 treats as more reliable, and D, because a loss estimated by the auditor with the activity's input is expected practice.
Final two: C beats A because a manager's explanation of the cause is a claim that needs corroboration in the file, while a dispute over a rating is not missing evidence.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, trace each part of a finding to its evidence; a fact that rests only on the audited manager's account needs corroboration before the finding goes out.

questions.subtopic: 4D5 Analytical review techniques. Testing a claim that complaints fell
questions.question: In an engagement on a Thai online grocer's customer service, the manager says complaints fell 30% this year, proving service improved. Which analysis BEST tests the claim for internal auditor Ploy?

options.A: Complaints per thousand orders, this year set against last year
options.B: The number of complaints in each of the past five years
options.C: This year's complaints against the target in the service plan
options.D: The grocer's complaints per thousand orders against a rival's rate

questions.key_concept: Pick the analysis that answers the objective: a raw count moves with volume, so a rate per unit of activity tests a quality claim.
questions.pre_read: Ask what else could make the complaint count fall, then pick the comparison that rules it out.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.1 requires information consistent with the objective, here whether this grocer's service improved this year. A raw count falls whenever orders fall, so complaints per thousand orders set against last year, a prior-period comparison Standard 14.2's considerations name, tests the claim. A rival's rate, the closest choice, shows how the grocer compares with another firm, not whether its own service changed.

wrong_explanations.B: A longer trend shows direction, but raw counts rise and fall with order volume, so five years of counts cannot separate better service from fewer orders.
wrong_explanations.C: A variance against target tests whether the plan was met. The target may itself ignore volume, and meeting it does not show whether service improved.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a rate per order fixes the volume problem, but a benchmark shows relative standing, not this year's change, and a rival may count complaints differently.

tips: Eliminate: B, because raw counts move with order volume however many years they cover, and C, because a variance against target answers whether the plan was met.
Final two: A beats D because the claim is about change this year, which a prior-period rate tests; a rival's rate shows relative standing, not change.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, pick the analytic that answers the objective; when a count can move with volume, compare a rate per unit of activity instead.

questions.subtopic: 4D1 Sources of engagement information. A reliable system record of every wire
questions.question: Internal auditor Youssef must learn whether wires over $50,000 at a Moroccan bank this year had a second approver; the treasury system, its controls tested effective, logs both users. Which method BEST serves?

options.A: Observe wire releases at unannounced times through the year
options.B: Walk through one wire release with the treasury officer
options.C: Review treasury's monthly reports of wires released by one person
options.D: Extract the year's wire records and test those above the limit

questions.key_concept: For whether a control operated every time over a period, a reliable system record of every instance beats watching some of them.
questions.pre_read: Ask which method covers the whole year, and what makes the records it would use trustworthy.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.1 asks for information that is relevant, reliable and sufficient. The objective covers the large wires for the whole year. Records the auditor extracts directly from a system with effective controls gain reliability on both counts, and testing all of them leaves nothing unseen, as the standard's considerations on complete populations support. Treasury's own reports, the closest choice, cover the year too, but the activity under review prepared them.

wrong_explanations.A: Watching releases is first-hand, but it covers only the moments seen. Where no record exists it is the best method; here the system logs every wire.
wrong_explanations.B: A walk-through of one release shows how the process is designed and how that wire went; it cannot show that every large wire this year had a second approver.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the reports cover the year, but treasury, the activity under review, prepared them; Standard 14.1 favors information obtained directly or from an independent source.

tips: Eliminate: A, because observation covers only the releases watched, not the whole year, and B, because one walk-through shows design and a single wire.
Final two: D beats C because both cover the year, but the auditor's own extract from a well-controlled system is stronger than reports the activity under review prepared.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, when two sources cover the same population, prefer the one the auditor obtains directly from a well-controlled system over the activity's own reports.

questions.subtopic: 4D6 Findings and their significance. A corrected one-off loss against an open gap
questions.question: Internal auditor Dara finds a $90,000 pricing error from a Cambodian distributor's finished migration, corrected and every price rechecked, plus $4,000 of unapproved overrides any clerk can still make. How should Dara BEST prioritize them?

options.A: The migration error, then the price overrides
options.B: Both equal, as each caused a loss
options.C: The overrides, then the migration error
options.D: Neither, until management ranks them

questions.key_concept: Significance weighs the likelihood and impact of the risk: a large loss whose cause is gone can matter less than a small, continuing gap.
questions.pre_read: For each finding, ask how likely it is to happen again and how far it could reach, not only what it has cost.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.3 requires significance to be judged by the likelihood of the risk and its impact, and findings ranked by it. The migration is finished, its error corrected and every price rechecked, so that risk is unlikely to recur. Any clerk can still override prices without approval, so that risk is likely, and its impact is not capped by the $4,000 found. Ranking by the larger past loss, the closest choice, confuses loss with risk.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the error cost more, but its cause is gone, so the risk is unlikely to recur. Significance weighs likelihood and impact, not past loss alone.
wrong_explanations.B: A loss in each case does not make two findings equal. Standard 14.3 weighs the likelihood and impact of each risk, and here they differ sharply.
wrong_explanations.D: Internal auditors evaluate significance and rank findings with the function's methodology; management's view is useful input but does not set the ranking.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a loss in each case does not make two risks equal, and D, because internal auditors rank findings, with management's view as input only.
Final two: C beats A because Standard 14.3 weighs the likelihood and impact of the risk; a corrected one-off error is unlikely to recur, while open overrides are not.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, rank findings by the risk they leave open, likelihood and impact together, not by the money already lost.

questions.subtopic: 4D9 Supervising the engagement. Moving a task to another auditor
questions.question: Engagement supervisor Catalina, the chief audit executive's delegate for approvals, moves a Colombian flower exporter's customs test, unchanged, mid-fieldwork from auditor Andrés, now on leave, to auditor Camilo. What MOST clearly must happen?

options.A: Camilo reperforms Andrés's finished steps before going on
options.B: The chief audit executive approves the switch before Camilo starts
options.C: Catalina names Camilo in the program and approves the change
options.D: Camilo goes on; with the test unchanged, the program stands as approved

questions.key_concept: The work program names who performs each task, so moving a task to another auditor changes the program and needs prompt approval.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the work program must contain, then whether this switch changes it.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.6 requires the work program to name the internal auditors assigned to each task, and to be approved before use and promptly when it changes. Moving the customs test to Camilo changes that assignment, so Catalina, as the delegate, names Camilo and approves the change. Carrying on because the test is unchanged, the closest choice, overlooks that who performs each task is part of the program.

wrong_explanations.A: Reperforming finished work is a review choice when that work looks weak, and nothing here suggests it. What this switch changes is the program's assignment.
wrong_explanations.B: The chief audit executive may delegate approval, and Catalina holds it. Waiting for the chief audit executive's own approval adds a step the Standards do not require here.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the test is unchanged, but the program must name who performs each task (Standard 13.6), so moving it to Camilo changes the program and needs prompt approval.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a change of auditor does not call for reperforming sound finished work, and B, because Catalina already holds the chief audit executive's delegated approval.
Final two: C beats D because the program names who performs each task, so a reassignment changes the program even when the test itself does not.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, any change to the work program, including who is assigned to a task, needs prompt approval from the chief audit executive or the delegate.
